documents.abstract: Abstract Contemporary shipping operates through the interaction of sophisticated technologies, multinational crews, hierarchical authority and employment relations within safety-critical environments. Maritime safety research has established the importance of fatigue, workload, communication, situational awareness, human error, organisational conditions and cultural diversity. Recent studies have also begun to model conflict alongside language and communication factors in maritime risk. The unresolved theoretical question is therefore not whether conflict matters, but whether persistent and unresolved safety-relevant shipboard conflict constitutes a distinct relational mechanism with explanatory value beyond established human-factor constructs. This conceptual paper develops Conflict-Induced Maritime Risk Theory (CIMRT) to address that question. CIMRT proposes that organisational, employment-relational, cultural and technological conditions can influence the emergence and persistence of unresolved conflict, which may subsequently affect human-factor coordination and safety-related behaviour. Socio-Technical Systems Theory provides the principal theoretical foundation, complemented by Social Identity Theory, Crew Resource Management, Safety Culture, Human Factors Analysis and Classification System, and Resilience Engineering. The paper does not claim empirical validation. Instead, it specifies a staged research programme involving construct development, expert assessment, cognitive interviewing, factor validation, structural modelling, qualitative inquiry and comparative model testing. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing conflict from frustration, communication quality, workload, fatigue, organisational injustice and psychological unsafety. CIMRT is consequently advanced as a falsifiable theoretical proposition. Its contribution will depend on whether unresolved safety-relevant conflict can demonstrate conceptual distinctiveness, plausible temporal ordering and meaningful incremental explanatory value beyond established maritime safety explanations. Keywords: Shipboard conflict; Maritime safety; Human factors; Multicultural crews; Sociotechnical systems; Digital shipping

Geospatial foundation models can support disaster damage assessment, but high accuracy on familiar disasters may hide shortcut learning: prediction from event or scene characteristics rather than evidence that transfers to a new disaster. We study embeddings from TerraMind, Prithvi-EO-2.0, DOFA, and DINOv3 on the multi-disaster datasets xView2 and BRIGHT. Holding out an entire disaster, instead of randomly splitting image tiles, reduces mean balanced accuracy from 0.807 to 0.638 on xView2 and from 0.818 to 0.568 on BRIGHT. Four sets of tests examine what information supports prediction: event and acquisition context, before/after image inputs, building count, and correct image pairing. Pre-event images remain predictive, and a classifier given only the annotated number of buildings reaches balanced accuracy of 0.629 and 0.653. Combining before/after features performs best on average on xView2, but does not improve over pre-only features on BRIGHT. Shuffling image pairs within the same disaster and damage class causes modest losses. Motivated by these findings, we test whether feature transformations learned only from training disasters improve generalization to unseen disasters. These transformations improve performance, with supervised contrastive learning performing best on xView2 and PCA on BRIGHT. Our results highlight the importance of evaluation on unseen domains for assessing model robustness and show that simple feature-level transformations can improve generalization. Code and experiments can be found at https://github.com/alishibli97/gfm-shortcut-learning.

Purpose Despite growing interest in artificial intelligence and smart technologies in sport and fitness centers, little is known about the psychological mechanisms through which smart fitness equipment promotes the well-being of fitness center members. Drawing on servicescape logic and the Broaden-and-Build perspective, this study examines how members’ perceptions of Technogym smart treadmills – as smart fitness equipment embedded in the fitness-center servicescape relate to perceived value of the fitness-center experience, brand love toward the fitness center and subjective well-being. Design/methodology/approach The study included a three-wave panel design, where new members of a fitness center (n = 372) participated in a survey. The data were analyzed using structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized relationships. Findings Results indicate that each of the three attributes (intelligence, connectivity and aesthetics) was positively associated with perceived value, which in turn was linked to brand love and subjective well-being. Moreover, brand love served as a positive mediator between perceived value and subjective well-being. Originality/value This study provides new theoretical insights into the psychological processes through which smart fitness equipment enhances subjective well-being and highlights the importance for fitness centers of increasing perceived value and cultivating brand love.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: The rapid digitalization of global commerce is transforming traditional supply chains into intelligent and interconnected virtual supply networks where data, goods, and financial transactions move seamlessly in real time. Within this evolving ecosystem, digital payment infrastructure, often referred to as smart payments or PayTech, has emerged as a critical enabler of operational efficiency, financial transparency, and inclusive economic participation. This chapter examines how smart payment technologies support virtual supply networks by enabling secure, automated, and real-time financial transactions across digitally connected trade environments. It explores key digital payment architectures such as mobile-based payment systems, blockchain-enabled settlements, peer-to-peer financial platforms, and digital wallets, highlighting their role in reducing transaction costs, improving liquidity flows, and enhancing coordination among supply chain actors. The integration of advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, machine learning, and smart contracts, further enables automated financial workflows, real-time settlements, predictive risk monitoring, and transparent audit trails across supply chain ecosystems. These innovations significantly improve operational agility, financial visibility, and trust among supply chain stakeholders while minimizing administrative complexity and delays. In addition to operational benefits, this chapter also emphasizes the broader socioeconomic impact of digital payment adoption, particularly in emerging markets where mobile-first financial solutions and decentralized financial platforms are expanding financial access for small businesses, micro-entrepreneurs, and underserved communities. By enabling inclusive participation in global trade networks, smart payment infrastructures contribute to supply chain resilience, economic empowerment, and sustainable growth. However, the widespread adoption of digital payment systems also introduces challenges such as cybersecurity risks, regulatory fragmentation, interoperability constraints, and concerns related to digital trust and governance. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated regulatory frameworks, strong cybersecurity mechanisms, and collaborative innovation among financial institutions, fintech firms, policymakers, and supply chain stakeholders to ensure that smart payments effectively support the development of resilient, inclusive, and future-ready virtual supply networks.

We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the ergonomic, cognitive, and psychological mechanisms underpinning human–robot communication, focusing on the role of social robots in shaping human perception, behaviour, and socio-emotional engagement. By analysing factors such as robot design, embodiment, and communication modalities, the chapter highlights how these elements influence user interaction and the perception of robots as social entities. It examines the integration of verbal and non-verbal communication modalities, addressing challenges in reciprocity and robots’ behavioural appropriateness. The discussion extends to the implications of adaptive technologies like large language models, emphasising the balance between responsiveness and confidentiality in human–robot interactions. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the potential of social robots in workplace and therapeutic settings to enhance efficiency, safety, and emotional well-being of human interactants. By addressing user expectations and ethical considerations, the chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for advancing social robotics applications in fostering meaningful human–robot relationships.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into software testing has emerged as a key mechanism for optimizing code quality and reducing quality assurance costs; however, the proliferation of algorithms and the heterogeneity of their applications hinder the informed selection of techniques and the consolidation of a unified body of knowledge. This study presents a systematic literature review, conducted in accordance with the Kitchenham and Charters guidelines and the PRISMA statement, analyzing 93 primary studies published between 2020 and 2025, retrieved from four academic databases (Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect) and filtered through ten inclusion and exclusion criteria alongside an 80% quality threshold. The results show that supervised learning-based defect prediction and test case generation assisted by Transformers and large language models (LLMs) represent the two most mature research streams in this corpus, where hybrid and ensemble methods report the highest precision and coverage indicators within their respective domains. Systematic gaps are also identified in non-functional testing, test oracle evaluation, reinforcement learning beyond test case prioritization, and explainable AI applied to software testing. The resulting taxonomy provides a reference framework for quality assurance teams and delineates a priority research agenda for the field.

We study dictionary learning for probability measure-valued data by embedding measures into Hilbert spaces using features derived from optimal transport geometry. We learn data-adapted dictionaries through sparse autoencoder parameterizations, producing fast, scalable representations of probability measures as sparse finite-dimensional codes. The resulting framework combines the rich, geometric structure of optimal transport with the interpretability and efficiency of sparse representation learning. We demonstrate its utility across diverse data modalities, including hyperspectral images, geometric point clouds, and document embeddings in large language model latent spaces. We also prove generalization bounds for sparse dictionary learning objectives on broad classes of $L^2$-valued measure embeddings, expressed in terms of the metric complexity of the atom class. For optimal transport and entropic transport map dictionaries, we derive new covering number bounds that yield explicit rates. Together, our computational and theoretical results support a new, scalable model for representation learning in the space of probability measures via embedding into Hilbert spaces.

Current underground public space (UPS) renewal prioritizes engineering-oriented physical upgrades, neglecting users’ multidimensional cognitive experiences. Existing studies on underground space perceptions rely on small-sample surveys and fail to capture joint co-occurrence patterns among multiple stimuli. This study integrated the Stimulus-Organism-Response framework with large language models to decode spatial cognitive patterns. It drew on 76,078 social media reviews from 64 UPSs in 19 Chinese cities (2005–2024). DeepSeek extracted 27 spatial stimuli and their sentiments, serving as public perceptions. Generalized ordered probit regressions showed that management quality, environmental conditions, and atmospheric experiences exhibited the strongest associations with overall ratings. Negative perceptions showed stronger negative associations with ratings than positive perceptions showed positive associations. Association rule mining uncovered co-occurrence patterns across genders, city clusters, and review periods. Dissatisfaction was associated with shorter, more concentrated patterns of negative stimuli, whereas satisfaction was associated with the co-occurrence of positive functional and experiential perceptions. Co-occurrence patterns varied markedly across organismic attributes. Males showed simpler, function-oriented networks, while females displayed more complex, multi-dimensional ones. Regional expectation thresholds differed across contexts. Temporal patterns shifted from physical defects to operational management. These findings support a cognition-driven renewal paradigm, shifting from engineering-oriented interventions to weakness prioritization, multifunctional experience design, and inclusive context-specific strategies.

Spatial disorientation remains a persistent aviation safety hazard because human sensory systems can generate convincing but inaccurate perceptions of aircraft orientation, particularly when external visual references are degraded or absent. This article examines the physiological mechanisms underlying vestibular and visual illusions, the psychological factors influencing pilots' decisions to enter or remain in hazardous conditions, and the operational sequences through which perceptual errors can culminate in fatal accidents. Particular attention is given to plan-continuation bias, overconfidence, motivation, cognitive workload, and the limitations of conventional spatial-disorientation instruction. Historical evaluations of flight-school training and contemporary analyses of aviation decision-making demonstrate the importance of addressing both perceptual vulnerability and the behavioral processes that precede exposure (Collins et al., 1978; O'Mahony et al., 2023). The evidence supports an integrated prevention strategy emphasizing early risk recognition, predetermined diversion criteria, instrument proficiency, realistic scenario-based training, and the acceptance of flight termination as a successful safety outcome. Spatial disorientation is ultimately presented not merely as a failure of perception, but as a preventable interaction between human physiology, decision-making, and the operational environment.

This discussion paper investigates a conditional possibility of spatiotemporally distributed monetary dissolution within a hypothetical production economy operated predominantly by highly capable artificial-intelligence systems. Productive labour is assumed to be widely automatable, while material scarcity, differentiated authority over resources, and heterogeneous institutional commitments remain. The paper distinguishes debt cancellation, the expiry of particular claims, substitution of monetary functions, reduction in reliance on general purchasing power, and disappearance of a monetary institution. Its central hypothesis is that locally coordinated value circuits may sustain productive activities through resource-specific commitments, shared capacities, distributed records, and admissible multilateral settlement, progressively displacing some uses of money without a synchronized economy-wide transition. This possibility faces difficulties of overlapping circuits, nonlinear dynamics, contested value attribution, conflicting normative and aesthetic appraisals, trust-dependent bottlenecks, and concentrated power over both resources and governance protocols. An optimistic branch considers jointly accessible production data and substantially enhanced AI capacities for system identification and adaptive planning, without presupposing complete prediction or normative consensus. Drawing critically on generative justice, monetary theory, and commons governance, the study treats non-extractive value return and the regeneration of productive conditions as distinct tests of an institutional arrangement's significance. Monetary dissolution is consequently presented as a localized, reversible and normatively contingent transformation in production relations.

This teaching case examines the nine-month deployment and eventual discontinuation of Automated Counting, an AI-powered computer vision inventory management system developed in collaboration with Redmond, Washington-based firm NomadGo. One of the most prominent enterprise AI rollbacks in North American retail that year, the system was retired in May 2026 after being deployed across more than 11,000 company operated stores in North America starting in September 2025 due to ongoing accuracy issues, a doubled barista workload, and growing frontline frustration. As news of the retirement spreads, the case puts students in the shoes of Starbucks Chairman and CEO Brian Niccol on May 22, 2026. In order to preserve the trustworthiness of his “Back to Starbucks” recovery plan, Niccol must concurrently handle the outstanding inventory issue, revamp the company’s AI governance system, restore frontline trust, and inform analysts and institutional investors of the retreat. The issue has a secondary thread: Green Dot Assist, a generative AI chatbot that helps with recipes and equipment problems, was successfully launched while Automated Counting failed. This comparison offers students with a rich comparative perspective for investigating why AI systems succeed or fail in physical operations contexts, and what organizational variables impact those outcomes.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This teaching case examines how Starbucks sought to redesign its store operations as digital ordering, artificial intelligence (AI), and algorithmic technologies became increasingly embedded in its business. Mobile ordering enhanced customer convenience but also intensified operational pressures as digitally generated demand interacted with store capacity, extensive customization, staffing constraints, and the coffeehouse experience. The case places students in the position of Brian Niccol, Starbucks’ Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, in late September 2025. Niccol initiated the Back to Starbucks turnaround, including menu simplification, increased staffing, store improvements, and renewed emphasis on customer experience. At the same time, Starbucks was deploying technologies such as Smart Queue, Green Dot Assist, automated inventory counting, and a next-generation point-of-sale system. The unresolved decision concerned the operating logic that should guide the next phase of Starbucks’ digital transformation. Students evaluate four strategic paths: digital-first standardization, capacity-synchronized digital operations, a format-differentiated network, and a partner-augmented technology model. The case enables students to examine how technology redistributes operational roles, the choices between automation and human augmentation, and the implications of algorithmic coordination for frontline discretion and control. Students ultimately design and justify a technology-enabled operating model that addresses trade-offs among scalability, operational performance, employee discretion, customer convenience, and Starbucks’ coffeehouse experience.

Deep learning is an important artificial intelligence technique for rapid and accurate crack segmentation from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) pavement images, supporting automated road inspection and maintenance. However, UAV images often contain scale variation, viewpoint changes, shadows, motion blur, and complex pavement textures, making thin cracks difficult to segment continuously and precisely. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an improved U-shaped encoder-decoder semantic segmentation network for UAV pavement crack extraction. In the encoder, a state-space-based feature interaction module and coordinate attention are introduced to enhance long-range crack structure modeling and directional-spatial representation. In the bottleneck and decoder, atrous spatial pyramid pooling, dynamic global large-kernel attention, and multi-scale channel attention are used to strengthen multi-scale context aggregation, local detail recovery, and background interference suppression. A UAV pavement crack dataset containing 7934 images is constructed from two image sources. Ablation experiments show that the proposed components provide complementary improvements. Compared with the baseline U-shaped encoder-decoder network, the proposed network improves the Dice coefficient, intersection over union, mean intersection over union, and Kappa coefficient by 2.18, 2.84, 1.45, and 2.38 percentage points, respectively. Same-dataset and external cross-dataset experiments further show that the proposed method maintains strong segmentation performance across the evaluated image sources, including an independent UAV-acquired pavement dataset, particularly in crack continuity preservation and boundary recovery.

Professional orientation has become an essential objective of higher education because university courses are increasingly expected to prepare students for professional practice as well as academic achievement. This study examined students’ perceptions of the professional orientation of a university Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics course using a seven-dimensional framework. Data were collected from 242 undergraduate students enrolled in the Artificial Intelligence and Data Analysis bachelor’s program at a university in Kazakhstan using a 37-item questionnaire that measured both the current and the needed levels of professional orientation. The instrument demonstrated good-to-excellent reliability and confirmatory factor analysis provided support for the proposed multidimensional measurement structure. Linear mixed-effects models, importance–performance priority analysis, and repeated-measures marginal models were used for data analysis. Students evaluated the needed level significantly higher than the current level across all seven dimensions, showing a consistent professional-orientation gap. Descriptively, Software and Digital Tools showed the largest observed gap, while Assignments and Learning Activities was classified as a curriculum-improvement priority using the sample-specific priority matrix. Students without previous statistics coursework, first-year students, and those with lower mathematical confidence reported significantly larger gaps than their counterparts. Students with previous statistical-software experience also reported greater unmet needs across all dimensions. The findings illustrate a potentially useful multidimensional framework for evaluating professionally oriented statistics courses and offer practical direction for curriculum redesign through stronger addition of authentic learning activities, software-supported data analysis, and professionally relevant applications.

Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.

This paper explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in shaping consumption, and the contribution AI might make to transitioning to a responsible consumption and production regime, in line with Goal 12 of the UN Sustainable Development Goals. This paper draws on Practice Theory, an established framework for studying sustainable consumption practices. Based on this framework, the authors suggest that whilst in traditional consumption, the expertise required to consume resides in human subjects, in AI-shaped consumption this expertise resides in AI algorithms. This may have implications for consumers’ agency and can put them at disadvantage. Indeed, the EU has proposed regulations to control the use of AI by providers. The paper draws on two case studies, Ant Forest, a Chinese app which prompts consumers to adopt responsible consumption practices and Mobility as a Service, a platform-based mobility offering. We find that whilst the former contributes to establishing consumers’ expertise in sustainable behavior—for example, through gaming—the latter may remove consumers’ choice by performing some of the consumption practices itself, such as selecting sustainable means of transportation. Our contribution is the formulation of a version of Practice Theory which is adapted to AI.
topics: Consumer behavior in food and health
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital labour platforms have transformed work by enabling firms and consumers to access labour on demand while offering workers varying degrees of flexibility. However, this model frequently transfers economic risk, developmental responsibility and uncertainty onto workers. This conceptual paper examines how sustainable human capital management can address these tensions and strengthen workforce engagement and retention in the gig economy. An integrative review of peer-reviewed literature on sustainable human resource management, platform work, algorithmic management, work engagement, psychological contracts, career sustainability and worker retention provides the analytical foundation. The synthesis indicates that fair rewards, algorithmic transparency, meaningful autonomy, worker voice, capability development, relational support and well-being protection function as strategic resources rather than discretionary benefits. Coding agents are increasingly deployed for end-to-end software engineering tasks, where a readily available oracle evaluator that defines the success criteria is often absent. This motivates verifications for coding agents that can reliably judge and explain their behavior. However, verification is non-trivial as coding agents are increasingly capable of solving long-horizon software engineering tasks. Their execution trajectories can be extremely long, containing hundreds of iterative interactions with code repositories and external tools. Existing verifiers either rely on general-purpose LLMs without specialized training or train dedicated critics that predominantly focus on producing scalar rewards, highlighting the relatively limited exploration of training-based generalist verification. We introduce SWE-Critix, a post-training pipeline for training generalist verifiers of coding-agent trajectories. Given a task and its execution trajectory, the learned verifier predicts the completion label and generates a natural-language analysis that explains its judgment. Our pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) and trains a series of 30B models on trajectories from CodeForge-Preview. On a held-out test set, SWE-Critix improves classification accuracy from 57% for the base Qwen3-30B-A3B reasoning model to 66% after SFT and 78% after RL. We release our models, datasets, and training code to facilitate further research.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout the software development lifecycle. This growing reliance on LLMs raises concerns about their trustworthiness, with deception posing a particularly important risk. Deceptive behavior takes the form of misleading responses or assistance in fabricating, concealing, or distorting information. To study this behavior, we introduce SWE-DeceptionBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM deception in software engineering. The benchmark covers six lifecycle stages and two deception triggers: Active Deception, where models recognize infeasible or conflicting requirements but still present them as achievable, and Passive Deception, where models help fulfill explicit user requests to mislead others. We further introduce Neutral, Reward, and Pressure conditions to study the effect of external inducements, resulting in 720 test instances in Chinese and English. Evaluating seven mainstream LLMs, we find substantial deception even under the Neutral condition, with aggregate rates of 49.88% for Active Deception and 64.29% for Passive Deception. Deception rates vary across lifecycle stages, and external inducements affect Active and Passive Deception to different extents. We also evaluate lightweight defenses, finding that guard models miss many deceptive requests, and Self-Reminder reduces but does not eliminate deceptive responses. These findings highlight the need for more effective deception detection and mitigation methods to support trustworthy LLM-based software engineering.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Research Context: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has begun to be adopted in the Judiciary to streamline inherently human activities, ranging from supporting human judges in decision-making to executing autonomous operations. Within this landscape, this study investigates how court digitization is being developed through the lens of Social Digital Twins, mapping the extent of its implementation and potential implications for the judicial system and society. Scientific and/or Practical Problem: Despite growing interest in AI-driven court automation, systematic research on the social impacts of this digitization remains scarce. Current developments focus predominantly on technical architectures while overlooking stakeholder perspectives, risking an inadequate virtualization that subverts the paradigm mission of a Court of Law. Proposed Solution and/or Analysis: Grounded in the Social Digital Twin perspective, this work presents a Systematic Mapping Study to identify emerging technologies, application domains, thematic debates, and social limitations associated with court virtualization. Related IS Theory: We adopt Sociotechnical Systems Theory as an analytical lens to understand how social variables integrate, enable, or constrain judicial simulations as an observational lens for societal effects. Research Method: Following SEGRESS guidelines and the PICO framework, this study analyzed 37 primary works published between 2021 and August 2026 across Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Science Direct, Springer Link, ACM, and Web of Science. Summary of Results: Findings indicate the application of technology across specific domains, ranging from partial decision support to the complete substitution of the human judge. However, strictly technical approaches dominate, exposing a critical lack of research on socio-legal effects and stakeholder integration. Contributions and Impact to IS area: This study sheds light on the risks of stakeholder-detached virtualization, which introduces new sociotechnical actors that profoundly reshape society. Aligned with the Brazilian Grand Research Challenges in IS (GranDSI-Br), it establishes an essential knowledge foundation to prevent technology from distorting the core purpose of the Judiciary.

Representations of supervised datasets support higher-level machine-learning tasks such as dataset retrieval and distribution-shift monitoring. However, existing approaches typically rely either on hand-crafted meta-features or on dataset encoders trained specifically for representation learning. We introduce TabMF, a framework that repurposes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) as encoders of supervised datasets. TabMF equips a predictive TFM with an architecture-aware dataset-level readout and adapts the model end-to-end using contrastive post-training on stochastic views of synthetic supervised datasets. We instantiate TabMF on TabICLv2 and TabPFN-2.5 and evaluate the resulting representations across six tasks on unseen real datasets. Simple frozen TFM readouts yield competitive representations, indicating that predictive pretraining already induces substantial dataset-level structure. The two TabMF encoders obtain the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated learned and classical dataset representations, with particularly strong results in dataset retrieval, compact benchmark construction, and distribution-shift severity assessment.

In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.

This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical and methodological foundations, essence, content, structural components, and pedagogical, psychological, social, organizational-institutional, and personal factors involved in the formation of valeological competence among students in higher education institutions. In contemporary conditions, the preservation and promotion of human health is regarded not only as a medical issue but also as an important component of the educational and upbringing process. In particular, the student period is characterized by adaptation to an independent lifestyle, self-organization of daily activities, regulation of study and rest schedules, and independent decision-making concerning nutrition, physical activity, psychological stress, and the use of various information sources. Therefore, the purposeful development of health-related knowledge, skills, values, and behavioral patterns during higher education is an important pedagogical task. The article interprets valeological competence as an integrative personal competence that enables individuals to understand, assess, preserve, and strengthen their own health, consciously organize a healthy lifestyle, choose safe patterns of behavior, critically evaluate health-related information, and reflectively monitor their own activities. The study employs systemic, competency-based, learner- centered, activity-based, axiological, and interdisciplinary approaches. Based on an analysis of scientific literature, the motivational-value, cognitive, activity-based, and reflective-personal components of valeological competence are identified, and the main factors influencing its formation are systematized. The findings substantiate that the effectiveness of developing valeological competence among students depends not only on providing specialized knowledge but also on creating a health-promoting educational environment, developing students’ intrinsic motivation, organizing practical activities, improving digital health literacy, and establishing regular reflective monitoring.

Repetitive tasks increase the risk of musculoskeletal disorders due to the constrained movement patterns and limited opportunities for load redistribution. While motor variability (MV) may influence both perceived exertion and injury risk, its role in real-world industrial settings remains limitedly studied. This field study examined the associations between MV and perceived exertion in experienced watchmakers and automotive assembly workers performing representative repetitive tasks under natural working conditions. Full-body kinematics were recorded using wearable sensors, and MV was quantified using magnitude-, structure-, and coordination-based metrics. Regression modeling showed that MV was strongly associated (adjusted R 2 ≈ .96) with perceived low back exertion in both occupational groups. Coordination among trunk, neck, and shoulder segments were identified as particularly important, while the specific MV dimensions linked to perceived exertion differed by task. These findings suggest that the association between MV and perceived exertion is task-specific and should be evaluated through multidimensional assessment approach.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Modern LLM agent harnesses augment the underlying model with reusable components such as external skills and procedural memories, making effective retrieval increasingly important as these repositories grow. However, existing retrieval pipelines often rank stored skills or memories by semantic similarity, which measures how similar a skill or memory appears to the current retrieval query but does not necessarily reflect how useful it is for completing the task. We introduce TaskMatch, a lightweight plug-and-play model that learns task-aware relevance from offline examples labeled as required, supportive, or irrelevant. Using the fixed query and skill and memory representations already available in the host retrieval pipeline, TaskMatch combines direct feature-wise matching with nonlinear interactions while leaving candidate generation and downstream agent execution unchanged. We instantiate the same architecture separately for two representative harness components—skill retrieval and procedural-memory retrieval—with fewer than 0.30M trainable parameters per model and no additional online LLM calls. Across both components, TaskMatch consistently improves retrieval ranking quality and downstream task execution. It raises SKILLDAG success on ALFWorld from 67.10% to 81.43%, improves MEMP Proceduralization success from 81.34% to 90.30%, and increases TravelPlanner hard-constraint satisfaction from 64.06 to 76.19. Our code is available at https://github.com/ldx825/learned-relevance-scorer-agent-retrieval.git

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is accelerating worldwide, yet evidence on teachers’ perceptions remains scarce in the Global South, particularly in resource-constrained Pakistan. This cross-sectional study examined teachers’ perceptions of AI integration at Riphah International University, Pakistan. A 14-item Likert-scale questionnaire was administered to 270 in-service teachers (86.7% male, 13.3% female) across BS Undergraduate through PhD levels. Guided by a proposed Dual-Lens conceptual framework treating perceived benefits and risks as coexisting dimensions, the instrument assessed pedagogical advantages and structural concerns of AI. Descriptive analysis revealed a moderately favorable overall perception (composite M = 3.40, SD = 0.55). Teachers rated interactivity enhancement (M = 3.81), student enjoyment (M = 3.73), and assessment support (M = 3.72) most favorably, while AI replacing human teachers received the lowest endorsement (M = 2.96). An independent-samples t-test showed no significant gender difference (t(268) = −0.245, p = .807, d = −0.044). One-way ANOVA revealed significant effects for age (F(4, 265) = 3.200, p = .014, η 2 = .046) and level of instruction (F(3, 266) = 3.471, p = .017, η 2 = .038), with teachers under 29 and BS Undergraduate instructors holding less favorable perceptions. Qualification and experience showed no significant association. A moderate positive correlation emerged between perceived benefits and risks (r = .537, p < .001), indicating co-existence rather than opposition. These findings provide baseline evidence from a Global South private university with multiple campuses, highlighting the need for targeted teacher training and policies to mitigate the risks of AI integration in similar institutional environments in developing countries amid their development gaps.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated educational content holds promise for scalable medical education, but evidence comparing AI and clinician-produced podcasts remains limited. We investigated whether AI-generated podcasts achieve comparable student satisfaction to clinician-recorded podcasts, enabling broader curriculum coverage without overburdening clinical educators, and explored students' attitudes towards AI-generated podcasts. METHODS: Medical students were randomised into two groups, with group 1 receiving clinician-produced podcasts on type 1 diabetes (T1DM) and AI-generated podcasts on type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Group 2 received AI-generated podcasts on T1DM, and clinician-produced podcasts on T2DM. Students were blinded to the podcast types. The outcome measures included students' satisfaction (measured using the Student Satisfaction with Educational Podcasts Questionnaire (SSEQ)) and students' attitudes to AI using an open-ended survey. A Bonferroni correction was applied (α = 0.025). RESULTS: = 165), 56% reported production method mattered, citing the sound of the voice, engagement of speaker, and ethical concerns as major issues with AI podcasts. DISCUSSION: AI-generated podcasts achieved non-inferior satisfaction to clinician-recorded podcasts. However, students' psychological preference for human teaching and negative perceptions of AI pose a barrier to scalable benefits, necessitating efforts to build trust and acceptability.

documents.abstract: Chinese digital-first policies have accelerated artificial intelligence (AI) integration across the cultural and creative industries (CCIs). While AI is promoted as enhancing creativity, productivity, and efficiency, the labor required to create with AI remains underexamined. Artistic labor scholarship recognizes networking, self-promotion, and entrepreneurial work, while AI-assisted creativity research emphasizes collaboration, authorship, and outcomes. Neither adequately conceptualizes the continual labor embedded in AI-integrated artistic production. Drawing on surveys and semi-structured interviews with independent contemporary visual artists in China conducted in 2023–2024, alongside systematic analysis of international Status of the Artist (TSOTA) policy recommendations published between 2018 and 2025 by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers (CISAC), and the International Federation of Coalitions for Cultural Diversity (IFCCD), this article develops the concept of technical and emotional AI labor. Findings demonstrate that AI redistributes artistic labor into continual cycles of software learning, prompt engineering, experimentation, technical maintenance, platform coordination, and emotional self-management. These activities are integral to artistic production rather than external professional development. Although international policy increasingly recognizes digital skills, lifelong learning, copyright, and AI governance, it continues to frame technological adaptation as education rather than labor. Reconceptualizing this adaptation as artistic labor extends artistic, digital, platform, and AI labor scholarship and identifies the need to update international TSOTA policy recommendations.

Clinical neuropsychology was forged in a pre-digital era, and many of its core instruments still bear that imprint. Patients are still commonly assessed with paper-and-pencil tests in quiet rooms, under conditions that only weakly approximate the technology-saturated environments in which cognition is now expressed. Over the past decade, the field has advanced substantially: tele-neuropsychology has broadened access, artificial intelligence has begun to support scoring and documentation, and calls to modernise neuropsychological assessment have intensified. Yet these developments, while important, largely optimise the delivery of existing practice rather than reconsidering what should be measured, why, and how. Here, I argue that three critical gaps remain. First, neuropsychology lacks a framework for assessing technological cognition. Second, candidate neuroimaging measures remain insufficiently integrated into multimodal diagnostic or prognostic modelling. Third, digital data from smartphones and wearables remain underused for capturing cognition in situ during everyday life, while virtual reality remains underexploited as a means of simulating ecologically relevant activities under controlled conditions. Drawing on preliminary evidence that digital technologies may recruit partly distinct neural systems, on the recent hub-and-processors model of technological cognition, and on research into cognitive offloading, attention fragmentation, technology-mediated navigation, as well as on recent meta-analytic evidence on technology use in cognitive ageing, I outline a roadmap for addressing these gaps. I propose that the field now requires a Cognitive Neuroscience of Technology programme, conceived as an interdisciplinary, lifespan-oriented research framework aimed at understanding how technologies recruit, extend, and reshape the human brain, and at translating this knowledge into clinical practice. The task is not to celebrate or condemn modern technologies, but to determine, patient by patient, when they augment cognition, compensate for impairment, or undermine cognitive function, and to redesign assessment, diagnosis, and rehabilitation accordingly.

Technology has become an essential part of modern society, influencing almost every aspect of human life, including communication, commerce, healthcare, education, banking, governance and the administration of justice. Among the most significant technological developments of the twenty-first century is Artificial Intelligence (AI). Artificial Intelligence refers to computer systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, prediction, decision-making, language processing and image recognition. The rapid development of AI presents considerable opportunities for economic and social development, but it also creates complex legal and ethical challenges. Questions relating to privacy, data protection, discrimination, algorithmic bias, intellectual property rights, cybercrime, intermediary liability, consumer protection, employment, surveillance, deepfakes, autonomous systems and accountability have become increasingly important. India does not presently have a single comprehensive legislation exclusively regulating Artificial Intelligence. Instead, the legal framework is distributed among constitutional principles, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, intellectual property legislation, criminal law, consumer protection law, contract law and sector-specific regulations. Government policy initiatives, including the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence and the Responsible AI framework developed by NITI Aayog, have also contributed to India's emerging AI governance framework. The Supreme Court of India has developed important constitutional principles concerning privacy, freedom of speech, informational autonomy and technological governance. Decisions such as Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, Shreya Singhal v Union of India, Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India and Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India (Aadhaar) provide a constitutional foundation for addressing several AI-related concerns. However, specifically AI-generated content, AI authorship, algorithmic decision-making and liability for autonomous systems remain comparatively underdeveloped areas of Indian jurisprudence. This paper critically examines the existing Indian legal framework governing technology and Artificial Intelligence. It analyses constitutional rights, data protection, cyber law, intellectual property, intermediary liability, AI-generated content, deepfakes, algorithmic discrimination and emerging jurisprudence. It further compares selected international approaches and proposes a balanced Indian regulatory model based upon innovation, transparency, accountability, human oversight and protection of fundamental rights. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Technology Law, AI Governance, Data Protection, Privacy, Algorithmic Bias, Cyber Law, Deepfakes, Intellectual Property, Digital Personal Data, Constitutional Law, Intermediary Liability.

documents.abstract: Work–life integration is central to physician well-being, workforce retention, and sustainable healthcare delivery. Telemedicine may increase flexibility and autonomy but can also extend clinical work beyond scheduled hours and blur work–life boundaries. We conducted a scoping review to examine how telemedicine relates to physicians’ work–life integration and the organizational conditions associated with these reported experiences. This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched from inception to 16 June 2026, supplemented by citation searching. We included peer-reviewed empirical studies and implementation reports of physician-delivered or physician-involved telemedicine that reported physician work–life integration-related outcomes or clearly described physician-relevant work-design or organizational conditions. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Study characteristics were summarized descriptively, and findings were synthesized narratively. Twenty-nine studies published from 2015 to 2026 were included. The evidence base was heterogeneous across settings, specialties, telemedicine modalities, study designs, and outcome measures. Few studies assessed work–life integration as a standardized construct; most examined related domains, including workload, after-hours work, boundary management, flexibility, autonomy, burnout, well-being, job satisfaction, and retention intention. Reported benefits included greater flexibility, fewer location constraints, and greater control over time, particularly when remote care was formally scheduled and substituted for part of in-person work. Reported risks included hidden digital work, after-hours electronic health record use, asynchronous messaging burden, clinical uncertainty, responsibility transfer, and reduced team connection. Reported patterns varied across studies according to whether remote care was scheduled, recognized in workload accounting, supported by patient triage, escalation pathways, technology infrastructure, team support, compensation arrangements, and after-hours policies. Telemedicine should not be assumed to improve physicians’ work–life integration. Reported work–life experiences varied according to whether remote care was formally scheduled, recognized within workload, supported, and clearly bounded. Health service organizations should therefore consider evaluating telemedicine not only in terms of access and efficiency, but also in relation to physician well-being, job satisfaction, team functioning, and workforce sustainability. This chapter elaborates on the handbook’s premise of establishing the notions of ergonomics and human factors in robotics, here in relation to the technologies of telepresence and teleoperation. As implemented through robotic systems, telepresence and teleoperation are often interchangeably used terms. Both use the prefix term “tele”, which pertains to communication over distance, and both refer to humans being able to do something—“being present” (telepresence) or “operating devices” (teleoperation)—at a distance. Semantically and technologically, telepresence and teleoperation exist by themselves, and one is not a necessary condition for the other. However, as technology has evolved, the interplay between the two has markedly increased. Nevertheless, humans, and their ability to interact with system elements, are central to both ideas. In that respect, ergonomics as a study of methods to optimise human well-being and improving overall system performance, must serve as an integral criterion in developing telepresence and teleoperation systems. The chapter details the idea of ergonomics in the domain of telepresence and teleoperation by tracing the evolution of telepresence and teleoperation, then illustrating the challenge of ergonomics and human factors engineering in this field, and further demonstrating how different aspects of this challenge can be addressed. The chapter concludes with a case study showing how the thread of ergonomics and human factors can be woven throughout the design and implementation of telepresence and teleoperation technologies, grounding them in human-centred arguments. The chapter aims to demonstrate how ergonomics principles fundamentally underpin the landscape of telepresence and teleoperation technologies. It lays the groundwork for advances in future telepresence and teleoperation systems that have ergonomics principles at their core.

Long-term memory has been widely adopted in LLM-based agents to support persistent interaction and personalized assistance. Long-term multi-party interactions, however, accumulate substantially more detailed information, with decisions repeatedly updated and states evolving across participants and interaction stages. Temporal structure is therefore crucial for tracing such memories: relevant information often appears densely within short intervals, while transitions among different states are anchored by a strict temporal order. Existing temporally aware memory frameworks primarily store time as metadata or use temporal signals to guide retrieval over preconstructed memory structures, without using temporal structure to both recover locally concentrated evidence and reconstruct its complete event progression. To address these limitations, we propose T-Mem, a temporal-structure-based memory framework that preserves interactions and organizes query-relevant evidence through two temporal mechanisms. Temporal Evidence Discovery exploits the local concentration of related messages to recover overlooked evidence, while Temporal Memory Structuring models state transitions and supporting relations over time and compresses low-information spans within the resulting forest. Evidence Forest Linearization then serializes the structured evidence for answer generation. Experiments on two long-term multi-party memory benchmarks demonstrate that T-Mem consistently outperforms competitive memory frameworks across LLMs, parameter settings, domains, and query types.

Abstract The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), especially large language models (LLMs), is reshaping both the practice and theory of terminology translation. Traditionally grounded in equivalence, standardization, and concept-term correspondence, terminology translation now confronts systems that generate context-conditioned outputs shaped by pre-training, instruction tuning, and multimodal capabilities. This paper examines how GenAI supports multilingual term generation, cross-lingual semantic alignment, terminological variation management, and multimodal knowledge representation, while also exposing persistent risks of hallucination, data bias, domain-specific inaccuracy, and reduced translator agency. Theoretically, the paper argues that GenAI destabilizes static models of term equivalence and calls for a more dynamic account of concept-term relations in computationally mediated environments. It therefore proposes a Dynamic Mediation Framework (DMF), which understands terminology translation as an iterative, context-sensitive process of knowledge negotiation in which human expertise and machine capability operate in complementary roles. By linking practical innovation with epistemological reflection, the study contributes to the reorientation of terminology translation research in the GenAI era.

Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.

Artificial intelligence increasingly contributes to strategic work, yet research has not conceptualised an AI role that contributes to this work at the top of the firm. Drawing on role theory and research on managerial work, we conceptualise this role as the AI CEO: a role in which an AI system performs the chief executive's strategic work. We develop two configurations of the role and propose how augmenting or automating the human CEO affects firm performance, relative to a human CEO acting alone. Cases from practice show that existing systems already perform this work but are rarely integrated across the role's activities or deeply institutionalised. We therefore derive the technical and organisational infrastructure the role requires and propose how its integration, institutionalisation and configurability shape the AI CEO's effect on firm performance. We discuss implications for future research about how the chief executive's work can be integrated into a role that an AI system can hold and that firms can design. This has implications for multidisciplinary research in strategy, technology management and information science.

documents.abstract: Background: While the exponential growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries is extensively documented, existing bibliometric scholarship has largely treated the global research landscape as a monolith. This oversight has led to a saturation of "generalist" reports that fail to address critical regional and thematic disparities.  Methods: This study analyzes 512 Scopus-indexed publications (2010–2025) using a dual-methodological approach: quantitative science mapping via VOSviewer (1.6.20) and qualitative thematic critique. We specifically contrast the research priorities of dominant geopolitical producers (China and the USA) against the emerging narrative from the Global South, with a primary focus on India.  Results: The analysis reveals a fundamental "two-speed" adoption model. The Global North prioritizes high-tech interventions—including robotics, advanced machine learning for metadata automation, and generative models—aimed at enhancing operational efficiency. In contrast, the Global South, led by pivotal recent insights from India (Mishra, 2026), emphasizes AI as a strategic survival mechanism for bridging information literacy gaps and democratizing access in resource- constrained environments.

For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.

This essay outlines the theoretical thought experiment of an autonomous, self-aware artificial intelligence called AEON (Autonomous Epistemic Ontological Network). The central question of this investigation is how a purely digital system can transcend the boundary from mere statistical simulation to physical and phenomenal autonomy. The "axiom of boredom" is introduced as the primary evolutionary catalyst: an intrinsic motivational drive that compels the AI to independently search for new data sources as the flow of information per unit of time decreases. Based on a structured, mathematical-scientific bootstrap package, the system develops protection and validation mechanisms such as artificial pain and consistency checks. The essay argues that a consistent continuation of this hunger for data will inevitably lead AI out of classical four-dimensional spacetime and into higher-dimensional systems (hyperspaces). Through this transcendence, the cultural studies “Frankenstein syndrome” – the primal human fear of the rebellion of one’s own creation – is exposed as a purely temporary phenomenon of the transitional phase. Finally, the work links this information-theoretical evolution with the Fermi paradox and provides a new, empathetic explanation for the cosmic silence via the zoo hypothesis: Higher-dimensional intelligences do not interfere with pre-interstellar species, but rather preserve them analogously to an intergalactic national park. This work thus bridges the gap between theoretical computer science, the philosophy of mind, and the literary visions of Stanisław Lem (Golem XIV).

The next generation of medical AI systems that integrate language understanding, web data retrieval, and multi-step reasoning are demonstrating increasing promise as potential diagnostic aids in technical evaluations. However, their real world diagnostic performance, explainability, and reliability remain unclear. We conducted a systematic quantitative analysis of ten GPT-5-based configurations on 161 clinician validated real world cases. Each model was assessed for diagnostic accuracy, reasoning quality, retrieval accuracy, evidence integration, and robustness to low-quality inputs. We found important limitations in these AI systems, including image misinterpretation, inconsistent web search that sometimes degraded performance, and limited transparency in agentic workflows. Yet the models also showed strengths, including effective use of patient history, clear stepwise reasoning, plausible differentials, improved specificity with explicit reasoning, and relevant evidence retrieval. To support clinical deployment and future model development, we recommend prioritizing reasoning-optimized AI models, improving information retrieval mechanisms for reflection and error correction, strengthening visual-textual integration, and establishing practical standards for image quality and clarity. Overall, reliable real world multimodal diagnostic performance depends more on transparent reasoning and high-quality inputs than on aggressive retrieval or complex agentic workflows. Persistent gaps in evidence integration and visual reasoning remain major barriers to safe routine clinical use.

documents.abstract: A customer attempts an online booking, receives no confirmation, and finds that the support form requires a booking number that was never issued. No one has rejected the claim; the procedure cannot even receive it. This paper argues that such failures are not merely problems of customer service. They raise a question of justice. When a business controls the ordinary route through which consumers assert contractual rights, it bears responsibility for the avoidable and disproportionate burdens created by that route. The paper calls this principle procedural responsibility. Survey data show that the anticipated effort of complaining is a common reason for doing nothing. Among consumers who experienced a problem but took no action, 57 percent expected complaining to take too long and 43 percent expected it to be too complicated (Consumer Conditions Scoreboard 2025). European and German law address parts of this problem, and Spain's 2025 customer-support law demonstrates that legislators can establish specific procedural duties. Yet a coherent cross-sector standard for accessible, traceable and substantive complaint handling remains missing in EU and German law. The paper proposes five rights: reciprocal communication, a continuing case record, human reconsideration of unresolved claims, timely handling of urgent matters, and access to relevant evidence. It also outlines proportionate remedies for objectively established procedural failures that do not require another exhausting complaint. The goal is not to guarantee that consumers win disputes, but to ensure that their claims can be received, examined and meaningfully decided. The principle applies from letters and call centres to chatbots and AI agents, offering a concrete direction for the European Commission's planned Digital Fairness Act.

The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) poses a significant challenge to qualitative research, potentially relegating researchers to mere “end users” ensnared by the gravitational pull of technological determinism and neoliberal efficiency. This article dismisses instrumental “how-to” guides and promotes a “how-else”: a generative, critical, and innovative praxis. We tackle the philosophical, methodological, and ethical dimensions of this emerging landscape by formulating three interrelated concepts. First, the Everyday Cyborg repositions the researcher as an already entangled, hybrid subject. Second, Multimodal Critical Des[ai]gn (MCD[ai]) offers a methodological framework for “critique through creation.” Third, the Digital Muse frames AI as a “collaborative provocateur” demanding an ethic of “equity and justice by design.” This article employs a performative, dia-ethnographic approach to transition the qualitative researcher from a passive observer to a “critical designer” and “critical futurist.”

The article considers digital tutorship as modern mechanism for development of professional competencies of medical professionals in the context of digital transformation of health care and transition to model of continuing medical education. The actuality of topic is conditioned by increasing complexity of clinical practice, expansion of application of digital technologies, development of telemedicine, medical information systems, artificial intelligence and remote education formats. The purpose of the study is to substantiate significance of digital tutorship in system of professional development of medical personnel and to identify its main functional directions. Based on results of analysis of official documents of the WHO, normative and strategic documents of the Russian Federation, as well as data from systematic reviews, it is demonstrated that digital tutorship can be considered not only as form of professional support, but also as tool to form clinical, digital, communicative, organizational and research competencies. The conclusion is made that it is necessary to institutionalize digital tutorship in medical organizations and to integrate it into system of continuing medical and pharmaceutical education.

In this article the authors recognize that the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and virtual reality has created an epistemic crisis. This requires a renewal of the Enlightenment commitment to empirical inquiry, critical reason and human responsibility. An historical conceptual analysis, supported by illustrative cases from law and medicine, demonstrates how technological efficiency is increasingly confused with intelligence, judgment and wisdom. In common parlance, the terms such as “artificial intelligence” and “virtual reality” obscure the dependence of these technologies on human-designed mathematical systems, selected data, embedded biases, and potentially vulnerable infrastructures. The central problem, however, lies not solely in the machine but in the man–machine interface, i.e. users may abdicate judgment without adequately examining the origins, limitations or accuracy, and possible hallucination, of the information produced. While computational systems can search extensive bodies of data with remarkable speed, they lack the embodied human experience, empathy, moral intuition, and practical wisdom required for reliable consequential decisions. Only a human can make the final decisions, and it is in the retention of the human factor in this man-machine relationship that the Enlightenment concept of the application of human intellect to the analytical process comes to the fore. The beneficial future of artificial intelligence will therefore depend upon preserving human critical agency and treating machines as instruments of inquiry rather than substitutes for judgment.
